claim: Most replicative helicases are hexameric, ring-shaped motor proteins that translocate on and unwind DNA.
source: Most replicative helicases are hexameric, ring-shaped motor proteins that translocate on and unwind DNA.
evidence: This is a statement of established scientific knowledge about replicative helicases.

claim: G40P by itself is a very weak helicase that stalls at barriers as small as a single GC base pair.
source: The high-resolution assay revealed that G40P by itself is a very weak helicase that stalls at barriers as small as a single GC base pair and unwinds DNA with the step size of a single base pair.
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data from the single-molecule fluorescence assay showing stalling at GC base pairs.

claim: G40P unwinds DNA with the step size of a single base pair.
source: The high-resolution assay revealed that G40P by itself is a very weak helicase that stalls at barriers as small as a single GC base pair and unwinds DNA with the step size of a single base pair.
evidence: This is supported by experimental data from FRET measurements showing discrete stall levels corresponding to single base pair steps.

claim: Binding of a single ATPγS could stall unwinding, demonstrating highly coordinated ATP hydrolysis between six identical subunits.
source: Binding of a single ATPγS could stall unwinding, demonstrating highly coordinated ATP hydrolysis between six identical subunits.
evidence: This is supported by experimental data showing linear dependence of stalling on ATPγS concentration.

claim: Frequent slippage of the helicase is observed.
source: We observed frequent slippage of the helicase, which is fully suppressed by the primase DnaG.
evidence: This is supported by experimental observations in single-molecule traces.

claim: Slippage of G40P is fully suppressed by the primase DnaG.
source: We observed frequent slippage of the helicase, which is fully suppressed by the primase DnaG.
evidence: This is supported by experimental data comparing slippage events with and without DnaG.

claim: Helicases are essential enzymes for all life forms.
source: Helicases are essential enzymes for all life forms and catalyze the separation of double-stranded nucleic acids (dsNA) into single-stranded nucleic acids (ssNA), and many of these enzymes involved in DNA repair, DNA recombination and transcription termination are linked to human diseases (Crampton et al., 2006; Enemark and Joshua-Tor, 2008; Enemark and Joshua-Tor, 2006; Gai et al., 2004; Johnson et al., 2007; Lionnet et al., 2007; Lohman et al., 2008; Manosas et al., 2009; Pandey et al., 2009; Patel and Picha, 2000; Rasnik et al., 2006b; Ribeck et al., 2010; Rothenberg et al., 2007; Singleton et al., 2000; Thomsen and Berger, 2009; Wang et al., 2008; Yodh et al., 2010).
evidence: This is supported by citations to multiple studies and represents established scientific knowledge.

claim: Helicases catalyze the separation of double-stranded nucleic acids (dsNA) into single-stranded nucleic acids (ssNA).
source: Helicases are essential enzymes for all life forms and catalyze the separation of double-stranded nucleic acids (dsNA) into single-stranded nucleic acids (ssNA), and many of these enzymes involved in DNA repair, DNA recombination and transcription termination are linked to human diseases (Crampton et al., 2006; Enemark and Joshua-Tor, 2008; Enemark and Joshua-Tor, 2006; Gai et al., 2004; Johnson et al., 2007; Lionnet et al., 2007; Lohman et al., 2008; Manosas et al., 2009; Pandey et al., 2009; Patel and Picha, 2000; Rasnik et al., 2006b; Ribeck et al., 2010; Rothenberg et al., 2007; Singleton et al., 2000; Thomsen and Berger, 2009; Wang et al., 2008; Yodh et al., 2010).
evidence: This is supported by citations and represents established knowledge about helicase function.

claim: Many helicases involved in DNA repair, DNA recombination and transcription termination are linked to human diseases.
source: Helicases are essential enzymes for all life forms and catalyze the separation of double-stranded nucleic acids (dsNA) into single-stranded nucleic acids (ssNA), and many of these enzymes involved in DNA repair, DNA recombination and transcription termination are linked to human diseases (Crampton et al., 2006; Enemark and Joshua-Tor, 2008; Enemark and Joshua-Tor, 2006; Gai et al., 2004; Johnson et al., 2007; Lionnet et al., 2007; Lohman et al., 2008; Manosas et al., 2009; Pandey et al., 2009; Patel and Picha, 2000; Rasnik et al., 2006b; Ribeck et al., 2010; Rothenberg et al., 2007; Singleton et al., 2000; Thomsen and Berger, 2009; Wang et al., 2008; Yodh et al., 2010).
evidence: This is supported by multiple citations to previous studies.

claim: Non-hexameric helicases with a pair of RecA-like domains are members of SF I and SF II.
source: Non-hexameric helicases with a pair of RecA-like domains are members of SF I and SF II, and are involved in DNA maintenance including repair, Holliday junction migration, chromatin remodeling, RNA melting and RNA-binding protein displacement.
evidence: This is a statement of established classification of helicases, supported by citation to Berger, 2008.

claim: SF I and SF II helicases are involved in DNA maintenance including repair, Holliday junction migration, chromatin remodeling, RNA melting and RNA-binding protein displacement.
source: Non-hexameric helicases with a pair of RecA-like domains are members of SF I and SF II, and are involved in DNA maintenance including repair, Holliday junction migration, chromatin remodeling, RNA melting and RNA-binding protein displacement.
evidence: This is supported by established knowledge about helicase functions.

claim: Hexameric or dodecameric helicases are classified into SF III-VI.
source: Hexameric or dodecameric helicases are classified into SF III-VI and are key players in DNA replication and transcription termination.
evidence: This is a statement of established helicase classification.

claim: Hexameric or dodecameric helicases are key players in DNA replication and transcription termination.
source: Hexameric or dodecameric helicases are classified into SF III-VI and are key players in DNA replication and transcription termination.
evidence: This is supported by established knowledge about helicase functions.

claim: SF III and SF VI helicases share a common fold called the AAA+ fold.
source: SF III and SF VI helicases share a common fold called the AAA+ fold and members of the SF IV and V share the RecA-like fold.
evidence: This is supported by structural knowledge of helicases.

claim: Members of the SF IV and V share the RecA-like fold.
source: SF III and SF VI helicases share a common fold called the AAA+ fold and members of the SF IV and V share the RecA-like fold.
evidence: This is supported by structural knowledge of helicases.

claim: Both AAA+ fold and RecA-like fold are structurally members of the ASCE (additional strand conserved E) superfamily of enzymes.
source: Both folds are structurally members of the ASCE (additional strand conserved E) superfamily of enzymes that consists of various multimeric enzymes with extremely diverse function (Erzberger and Berger, 2006).
evidence: This is supported by citation to Erzberger and Berger, 2006.

claim: The ASCE superfamily consists of various multimeric enzymes with extremely diverse function.
source: Both folds are structurally members of the ASCE (additional strand conserved E) superfamily of enzymes that consists of various multimeric enzymes with extremely diverse function (Erzberger and Berger, 2006).
evidence: This is supported by citation to Erzberger and Berger, 2006.

claim: Forward translocation of ring-shaped helicases on nucleic acids lattice is promoted by ATP hydrolysis.
source: Forward translocation of ring-shaped helicases on nucleic acids lattice is promoted by ATP hydrolysis.
evidence: This is established knowledge about helicase mechanism.

claim: Two distinct models have been proposed concerning how the hydrolysis of ATP molecules in a multi-subunit enzyme is coordinated between the subunits: a sequential, 'staircase-like' model for ATP hydrolysis and a concerted ATP hydrolysis model.
source: Based on crystal structures, two distinct models have been proposed concerning how the hydrolysis of ATP molecules in a multi-subunit enzyme is coordinated between the subunits: a sequential, 'staircase-like' model for ATP hydrolysis and a concerted ATP hydrolysis model.
evidence: This is supported by inference from crystal structures mentioned in the text.

claim: The staircase model is based on the structures of BPV E1 helicase bound to ssDNA and E. coli Rho helicase bound to ssRNA.
source: The staircase model based on the structures of BPV E1 helicase bound to ssDNA and E. coli Rho helicase bound to ssRNA (Enemark and Joshua-Tor, 2006; Thomsen and Berger, 2009) entails sequential hydrolysis of ATP around the hexameric ring, and one nt translocation for every ATP hydrolyzed.
evidence: This is supported by citations to structural studies.

claim: The staircase model entails sequential hydrolysis of ATP around the hexameric ring, and one nt translocation for every ATP hydrolyzed.
source: The staircase model based on the structures of BPV E1 helicase bound to ssDNA and E. coli Rho helicase bound to ssRNA (Enemark and Joshua-Tor, 2006; Thomsen and Berger, 2009) entails sequential hydrolysis of ATP around the hexameric ring, and one nt translocation for every ATP hydrolyzed.
evidence: This is an inference from structural data cited in the text.

claim: The unwinding step size has been proposed to be one base pair by extension of the staircase model, but this has not been experimentally tested.
source: By extension, the unwinding step size has been proposed to be one base pair (bp) but this has not been experimentally tested.
evidence: This is a statement about the lack of experimental evidence for a proposed model.

claim: The concerted hydrolysis model is based on the all-or-nothing nucleotide occupancy of SV40 Large T antigen structures.
source: The concerted hydrolysis model based on the all-or-nothing nucleotide occupancy of SV40 Large T antigen structures (Gai et al., 2004) posits that the six ATP binding sites fire simultaneously, moving on the DNA by an increment determined by the stroke size of the DNA binding motif, which can be larger than 1 nt or 1 bp.
evidence: This is supported by citation to structural studies.

claim: The concerted hydrolysis model posits that the six ATP binding sites fire simultaneously, moving on the DNA by an increment determined by the stroke size of the DNA binding motif, which can be larger than 1 nt or 1 bp.
source: The concerted hydrolysis model based on the all-or-nothing nucleotide occupancy of SV40 Large T antigen structures (Gai et al., 2004) posits that the six ATP binding sites fire simultaneously, moving on the DNA by an increment determined by the stroke size of the DNA binding motif, which can be larger than 1 nt or 1 bp.
evidence: This is an inference from structural data cited in the text.

claim: For T7 gp4 helicase-primase, structural and ensemble kinetic data suggested a sequential hydrolysis mechanism during DNA translocation.
source: For T7 gp4 helicase-primase, structural and ensemble kinetic data (Crampton et al., 2006; Liao et al., 2005; Singleton et al., 2000) suggested a sequential hydrolysis mechanism during DNA translocation, and with the one-to-one coupling between nucleotide unwinding and base pair unwinding (Pandey and Patel, 2014), but the estimated unwinding step size is either larger than 1 bp (Johnson et al., 2007) or is variable depending on the GC content of the duplex DNA (Donmez and Patel, 2008; Syed et al., 2014).
evidence: This is supported by citations to structural and kinetic studies.

claim: For T7 gp4, there is one-to-one coupling between nucleotide unwinding and base pair unwinding.
source: For T7 gp4 helicase-primase, structural and ensemble kinetic data (Crampton et al., 2006; Liao et al., 2005; Singleton et al., 2000) suggested a sequential hydrolysis mechanism during DNA translocation, and with the one-to-one coupling between nucleotide unwinding and base pair unwinding (Pandey and Patel, 2014), but the estimated unwinding step size is either larger than 1 bp (Johnson et al., 2007) or is variable depending on the GC content of the duplex DNA (Donmez and Patel, 2008; Syed et al., 2014).
evidence: This is supported by citation to Pandey and Patel, 2014.

claim: The estimated unwinding step size for T7 gp4 is either larger than 1 bp or is variable depending on the GC content of the duplex DNA.
source: For T7 gp4 helicase-primase, structural and ensemble kinetic data (Crampton et al., 2006; Liao et al., 2005; Singleton et al., 2000) suggested a sequential hydrolysis mechanism during DNA translocation, and with the one-to-one coupling between nucleotide unwinding and base pair unwinding (Pandey and Patel, 2014), but the estimated unwinding step size is either larger than 1 bp (Johnson et al., 2007) or is variable depending on the GC content of the duplex DNA (Donmez and Patel, 2008; Syed et al., 2014).
evidence: This is supported by citations to multiple studies showing conflicting results.

claim: Rho helicase is proposed to move in one nt steps.
source: For the Rho helicase proposed to move in one nt steps (Thomsen and Berger, 2009), chemical interference data suggest that Rho needs to reset itself after it unwinds about ~7 bp (Schwartz et al., 2009).
evidence: This is supported by citation to Thomsen and Berger, 2009.

claim: Chemical interference data suggest that Rho needs to reset itself after it unwinds about ~7 bp.
source: For the Rho helicase proposed to move in one nt steps (Thomsen and Berger, 2009), chemical interference data suggest that Rho needs to reset itself after it unwinds about ~7 bp (Schwartz et al., 2009).
evidence: This is supported by citation to Schwartz et al., 2009.

claim: For DnaB, ensemble kinetic studies supported a sequential ATP hydrolysis mechanism.
source: For DnaB, ensemble kinetic studies supported a sequential ATP hydrolysis mechanism (Roychowdhury et al., 2009) with an unwinding step size of 1 bp (Galletto et al., 2004), but DnaB structure bound to ssDNA showed that one subunit of DnaB hexamer binds two nucleotides, leading to the proposal that DnaB unwinds DNA in two base pair steps (Itsathitphaisarn et al., 2012).
evidence: This is supported by citation to Roychowdhury et al., 2009.

claim: For DnaB, the unwinding step size was determined to be 1 bp by ensemble kinetic studies.
source: For DnaB, ensemble kinetic studies supported a sequential ATP hydrolysis mechanism (Roychowdhury et al., 2009) with an unwinding step size of 1 bp (Galletto et al., 2004), but DnaB structure bound to ssDNA showed that one subunit of DnaB hexamer binds two nucleotides, leading to the proposal that DnaB unwinds DNA in two base pair steps (Itsathitphaisarn et al., 2012).
evidence: This is supported by citation to Galletto et al., 2004.

claim: DnaB structure bound to ssDNA showed that one subunit of DnaB hexamer binds two nucleotides.
source: For DnaB, ensemble kinetic studies supported a sequential ATP hydrolysis mechanism (Roychowdhury et al., 2009) with an unwinding step size of 1 bp (Galletto et al., 2004), but DnaB structure bound to ssDNA showed that one subunit of DnaB hexamer binds two nucleotides, leading to the proposal that DnaB unwinds DNA in two base pair steps (Itsathitphaisarn et al., 2012).
evidence: This is supported by citation to structural study Itsathitphaisarn et al., 2012.

claim: Based on DnaB structure, it has been proposed that DnaB unwinds DNA in two base pair steps.
source: For DnaB, ensemble kinetic studies supported a sequential ATP hydrolysis mechanism (Roychowdhury et al., 2009) with an unwinding step size of 1 bp (Galletto et al., 2004), but DnaB structure bound to ssDNA showed that one subunit of DnaB hexamer binds two nucleotides, leading to the proposal that DnaB unwinds DNA in two base pair steps (Itsathitphaisarn et al., 2012).
evidence: This is an inference from structural data cited in the text.

claim: The DNA packaging motor from ϕ29 was shown to package dsDNA in a hierarchy of non-integer, 2.5 bp steps, pausing after packaging 10 bp.
source: In the most comprehensive analysis of stepping by a ring-shaped motor on DNA, the DNA packaging motor from ϕ29 was shown to package dsDNA in a hierarchy of non-integer, 2.5 bp steps, pausing after packaging 10 bp (Moffitt et al., 2009).
evidence: This is supported by citation to Moffitt et al., 2009.

claim: G40P is a DnaB type hexameric helicase.
source: We probed the helicase activity of the phage SPP1 G40P, a DnaB type hexameric helicase (Berger, 2008; Pedré et al., 1994; Wang et al., 2008) required for phage replication in its bacterial host, using an unwinding assay (Ha et al., 2002; Myong et al., 2007; Pandey et al., 2009; Syed et al., 2014; Yodh et al., 2009) based on single-molecule FRET (Ha et al., 1996).
evidence: This is supported by citations to previous studies.

claim: G40P is required for phage replication in its bacterial host.
source: We probed the helicase activity of the phage SPP1 G40P, a DnaB type hexameric helicase (Berger, 2008; Pedré et al., 1994; Wang et al., 2008) required for phage replication in its bacterial host, using an unwinding assay (Ha et al., 2002; Myong et al., 2007; Pandey et al., 2009; Syed et al., 2014; Yodh et al., 2009) based on single-molecule FRET (Ha et al., 1996).
evidence: This is supported by citations to previous studies.

claim: The substrate is a 40 bp duplex DNA with 3' and 5' single stranded poly-dT tails, both 31 nt long, to mimic a replication fork.
source: The substrate is a 40 bp duplex DNA with 3' and 5' single stranded poly-dT tails, both 31 nt long, to mimic a replication fork, and is immobilized to a polymer-passivated surface via a biotin-neutravidin linker (Figure 1a).
evidence: This describes the experimental design and is shown in Figure 1a.

claim: FRET between the donor (Cy3) and the acceptor (Cy5) fluorophores conjugated to the fork was used to follow individual DNA unwinding in real time.
source: FRET between the donor (Cy3) and the acceptor (Cy5) fluorophores conjugated to the fork was used to follow individual DNA unwinding in real time (Figure 1—figure supplement 1).
evidence: This describes the experimental method used.

claim: Duplex unwinding increases the time-averaged distance between the fluorophores therefore causing a reduction in FRET.
source: Duplex unwinding increases the time-averaged distance between the fluorophores therefore causing a reduction in FRET, and unwinding completion results in the release of the donor-labeled strand from the surface and an abrupt disappearance of total fluorescence (Figure 1b and Figure 1—figure supplement 1).
evidence: This is an inference from the FRET mechanism and is supported by data shown in figures.

claim: Unwinding completion results in the release of the donor-labeled strand from the surface and an abrupt disappearance of total fluorescence.
source: Duplex unwinding increases the time-averaged distance between the fluorophores therefore causing a reduction in FRET, and unwinding completion results in the release of the donor-labeled strand from the surface and an abrupt disappearance of total fluorescence (Figure 1b and Figure 1—figure supplement 1).
evidence: This is supported by experimental observations shown in the figures.

claim: Typical unwinding trajectories of all AT base pairs displayed a smooth and rapid FRET decrease at 1 mM ATP.
source: Initial experiments were carried out using a DNA substrate with all AT base pairs (40 bp) and typical unwinding trajectories displayed a smooth and rapid FRET decrease at 1 mM ATP (Figure 1c).
evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 1c.

claim: The kinetic step size of G40P on all AT substrate is ~4 bp.
source: Fitting the unwinding time histogram with a Gamma distribution allowed us to estimate a kinetic step size of ~4 bp, obtained by dividing the number of bp unwound by the number of identical rate-limiting steps required for full unwinding (Park et al., 2010) (Figure 1—figure supplement 1).
evidence: This is derived from data analysis using Gamma distribution fitting.

claim: The kinetic step size of 4 bp should be considered an upper limit because unwinding time distributions can be broadened due to molecular heterogeneities.
source: The kinetic step size of 4 bp here should be considered an upper limit because these unwinding time distributions can be broadened due to molecular heterogeneities, likely leading to an overestimation of the kinetic step size (Park et al., 2010).
evidence: This is an inference based on known limitations of the analysis method, supported by citation.

claim: When a single GC bp was inserted in the 11th position, a large fraction (65%) of unwinding trajectories showed a stall before full unwinding.
source: Interestingly, when we repeated the experiment with a single GC bp inserted in the 11th position in otherwise all AT sequences (Figure 1a), a large fraction (65%) of unwinding trajectories showed a stall before full unwinding, with a characteristic stall lifetime of 79 ± 5 ms (Figure 1d and Figure 1—figure supplement 2a).
evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in the figures.

claim: The characteristic stall lifetime at a single GC base pair is 79 ± 5 ms.
source: Interestingly, when we repeated the experiment with a single GC bp inserted in the 11th position in otherwise all AT sequences (Figure 1a), a large fraction (65%) of unwinding trajectories showed a stall before full unwinding, with a characteristic stall lifetime of 79 ± 5 ms (Figure 1d and Figure 1—figure supplement 2a).
evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 1—figure supplement 2a.

claim: FRET efficiencies of the stalled state at a single GC bp were sharply distributed around EFRET = 0.52 ± 0.04.
source: FRET efficiencies of the stalled state were sharply distributed around EFRET = 0.52 ± 0.04 (blue lines in Figure 1g), indicating that the stall occurs after a well-defined number of base pairs, presumably ten, have been unwound and is caused by a single GC base pair.
evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 1g.

claim: The stall at a single GC bp occurs after a well-defined number of base pairs, presumably ten, have been unwound.
source: FRET efficiencies of the stalled state were sharply distributed around EFRET = 0.52 ± 0.04 (blue lines in Figure 1g), indicating that the stall occurs after a well-defined number of base pairs, presumably ten, have been unwound and is caused by a single GC base pair.
evidence: This is an inference from the sharp distribution of FRET values and the position of the GC bp.

claim: Individual traces revealed helicase slippage events, where partial unwinding is reverted before another unwinding attempt is made.
source: Individual traces revealed helicase slippage events, where partial unwinding is reverted before another unwinding attempt is made (Figure 1d, lower panel).
evidence: This is supported by experimental observations shown in Figure 1d.

claim: The lag time between successive unwinding attempts is less than 1 s on average, which is about 20-fold shorter than the de novo unwinding initiation time.
source: The lag time between successive unwinding attempts is less than 1 s on average, which is about 20-fold shorter than the de novo unwinding initiation time (see Materials and methods and Figure 1—figure supplement 1d), implying that the same enzyme is responsible for multiple partial unwinding and slippage events (Ha et al., 2002; Sun et al., 2011).
evidence: This is supported by experimental data and comparison with initiation time.

claim: The same enzyme is responsible for multiple partial unwinding and slippage events.
source: The lag time between successive unwinding attempts is less than 1 s on average, which is about 20-fold shorter than the de novo unwinding initiation time (see Materials and methods and Figure 1—figure supplement 1d), implying that the same enzyme is responsible for multiple partial unwinding and slippage events (Ha et al., 2002; Sun et al., 2011).
evidence: This is an inference from the short lag time between attempts, supported by citations.

claim: In most slippage events followed by another unwinding attempt, the FRET efficiency returned to its original high value of DNA itself, indicating that the helicase slips backwards at least 10 base pairs.
source: In most slippage events followed by another unwinding attempt, the FRET efficiency returned to its original high value of DNA itself, indicating that the helicase slips backwards at least 10 base pairs.
evidence: This is an inference from the FRET efficiency returning to the original value.

claim: T7gp4 helicase was observed to slip backwards hundreds of base pairs in unfavorable nucleotide conditions.
source: Interestingly, T7gp4 helicase was observed to slip backwards hundreds of base pairs in unfavorable nucleotide conditions (Sun et al., 2011).
evidence: This is supported by citation to Sun et al., 2011.

claim: DNA with 2 GC bp (11th and 12th bp) showed stalls at two distinct FRET levels (EFRET = 0.53 ± 0.04 and EFRET = 0.39 ± 0.04).
source: DNA with 2 GC bp (11th and 12th bp) showed stalls at two distinct FRET levels (EFRET = 0.53 ± 0.04 and EFRET = 0.39 ± 0.04) determined from Gaussian fitting of EFRET distribution of stalled states (Figure 1h).
evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 1h.

claim: The first stall with 2 GC bp occurred at the same FRET level as observed with 1 GC bp.
source: Because the first stall occurred at the same FRET level as observed with 1 GC bp, we attribute the second stall to the second GC bp.
evidence: This is an inference from comparing FRET levels between different substrates.

claim: Two GC bp reduced full unwinding events to 57% of the traces.
source: Two GC bp reduced full unwinding events to 57% of the traces.
evidence: This is supported by experimental data.

claim: Complete unwinding trajectories were 12% for the DNA with 3 GC bp (11th, 12th and 13th bp).
source: Complete unwinding trajectories were even rarer (12%) for the DNA with 3 GC bp (11th, 12th and 13th bp).
evidence: This is supported by experimental data.

claim: Stalls with 3 GC bp are distributed in three distinct FRET levels with two main peaks centered at EFRET = 0.52 ± 0.04 and EFRET = 0.38 ± 0.04 and a small peak at EFRET = 0.27 ± 0.04.
source: Stalls were identified from all traces, predominantly from unsuccessful unwinding attempts and are distributed in three distinct FRET levels with two main peaks centered at EFRET = 0.52 ± 0.04 and EFRET = 0.38 ± 0.04 and a small peak at EFRET = 0.27 ± 0.04 (Figure 1i).
evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 1i.

claim: Crystallographic structures on ring-shaped helicases suggest step sizes between one and six nucleotides.
source: The aforementioned crystallographic structures on ring-shaped helicases suggest step sizes between one and six nucleotides, resulting from a staircase like or spring-loaded or concerted ATP hydrolysis model (Enemark and Joshua-Tor, 2006; Gai et al., 2004; Itsathitphaisarn et al., 2012).
evidence: This is supported by citations to structural studies.

claim: Recent experimental studies have reported for hexameric helicases step sizes from one to three nucleotides depending on the GC content of the template.
source: Recent experimental studies have reported for hexameric helicases step sizes from one to three nucleotides depending on the GC content of the template (Syed et al., 2014).
evidence: This is supported by citation to Syed et al., 2014.

claim: One, two or three discrete FRET values of stalled states induced by one, two or three GC base pairs suggest that unwinding occurs in single base pair steps.
source: One, two or three discrete FRET values of stalled states in our data induced by one, two or three GC base pairs suggest that unwinding occurs in single base pair steps.
evidence: This is an inference from the pattern of discrete FRET values observed.

claim: A calibration curve was obtained between the number of base pairs unwound and the FRET efficiency using four different DNA constructs that have m AT base pairs followed by (40-m) GC base pairs (m = 4, 7, 10 and 13).
source: As a further test, we obtained a calibration curve between the number of base pairs unwound and the FRET efficiency by performing the reaction using four different DNA constructs that have m AT base pairs followed by (40 m) GC base pairs (m = 4, 7, 10 and 13), which stalls the unwinding reaction presumably at the boundary between AT and GC base pairs (Figure 1j).
evidence: This describes the experimental approach for calibration.

claim: The stall FRET levels from the one, two and three consecutive GC base pairs fall within error in single base pair steps on the calibration curve.
source: The stall FRET levels from the one, two and three consecutive GC base pairs fall within error in single base pair steps on our calibration curve (see Materials and methods and Figure 1—figure supplement 2).
evidence: This is supported by comparison of experimental data with the calibration curve.

claim: Recent optical trap studies of the nonhexameric helicase HCV NS3 and XPD observed single base pair steps during unwinding.
source: Recent optical trap studies of the nonhexameric helicase HCV NS3 and XPD observed the long anticipated single base pair steps during unwinding (Cheng et al., 2011; Qi et al., 2013).
evidence: This is supported by citations to optical trap studies.

claim: Changing the solution condition from 10 mM MgCl2 to 10 mM CaCl2 slowed down unwinding significantly.
source: However, changing the solution condition from 10 mM MgCl2 to 10 mM CaCl2, slowed down unwinding significantly and allowed in the all AT substrate direct observation of individual steps, which occurred at similar FRET values to those observed for the GC bp induced pauses (Figure 1—figure supplement 3), consistent with single bp unwinding of AT base pairs.
evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 1—figure supplement 3.

claim: In CaCl2 conditions, individual steps in the all AT substrate occurred at similar FRET values to those observed for the GC bp induced pauses, consistent with single bp unwinding of AT base pairs.
source: However, changing the solution condition from 10 mM MgCl2 to 10 mM CaCl2, slowed down unwinding significantly and allowed in the all AT substrate direct observation of individual steps, which occurred at similar FRET values to those observed for the GC bp induced pauses (Figure 1—figure supplement 3), consistent with single bp unwinding of AT base pairs.
evidence: This is an inference from comparing FRET values under different conditions.

claim: The GC base pair induced pauses of the helicase imply that unwinding depends at least partially on the thermal fraying of the base pairs due to the higher thermodynamic stability of GC vs AT base pairs.
source: The GC base pair induced pauses of the helicase imply that unwinding depends at least partially on the thermal fraying of the base pairs due to the higher thermodynamic stability of GC vs AT base pairs.
evidence: This is an inference from the observation that GC base pairs cause stalling.

claim: Raising the experiment temperature increased the percentage of full unwinding events for the three GC bp construct from 12% at 21°C to 62% at 33°C.
source: Raising the experiment temperature increased the percentage of full unwinding events for the three GC bp construct, that is 62% vs. 12% at 33°C vs. 21°C, respectively (Supplementary file 1 - Table S2 and Figure 1—figure supplement 2b).
evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in Supplementary file 1 - Table S2 and Figure 1—figure supplement 2b.

claim: Structural studies of DnaB showed each DNA binding loop contacting two nucleotides.
source: Interestingly, structural studies of DnaB showed each DNA binding loop contacting two nucleotides (Itsathitphaisarn et al., 2012), leading to the step size of 2 bp.
evidence: This is supported by citation to structural study.

claim: Single-molecule studies of T7gp4 observed 2–3 bp apparent step sizes but with the step likely requiring 2–3 nucleotides hydrolyzed.
source: Single-molecule studies of T7gp4 observed 2–3 bp apparent step sizes but with the step likely requiring 2–3 nucleotides hydrolyzed (Syed et al., 2014).
evidence: This is supported by citation to Syed et al., 2014.

claim: G40P may possess variable step size, depending on the load, and under experimental conditions that slow down translocation, G40P may switch to a 1 bp step size.
source: Therefore, we could also imagine that G40P possesses variable step size, depending on the load, and under our experimental conditions that slow down translocation, G40P may switch to a 1 bp step size.
evidence: This is speculation based on the experimental observations.

claim: Gear switching was proposed for other ring-like ATPases, for example the AAA+ protease ClpXP and dynein.
source: Gear switching was also proposed for other ring-like ATPases, for example the AAA+ protease ClpXP (Sen et al., 2013) and dynein (Mallik et al., 2004).
evidence: This is supported by citations to studies on other ATPases.

claim: DnaG, the host primase, stimulates ATPase and unwinding activities of DnaB and G40P.
source: Because DnaG, the host primase, stimulates ATPase and unwinding activities of DnaB and G40P (Bird et al., 2000; Wang et al., 2008), we tested the effect of DnaG by forming a complex of G40P with the Bacillus subtilis primase DnaG in a ratio of 1:3 (Wang et al., 2008) before adding the complex to the immobilized DNA to initiate unwinding.
evidence: This is supported by citations to previous studies.

claim: The yield of complete unwinding increased from 12% without DnaG to 58% with DnaG for the substrate with 3 GC bp.
source: Strikingly, the yield of complete unwinding increased from 12% without DnaG to 58% with DnaG (Figure 3b and Supplementary file 1 - Table S1).
evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 3b and Supplementary file 1 - Table S1.

claim: DNA molecules showing full unwinding with DnaG did not show any slippage events.
source: DNA molecules showing full unwinding did not show any slippage events, suggesting a novel function of DnaG that stimulates unwinding by preventing slippage.
evidence: This is supported by experimental observations.

claim: DnaG stimulates unwinding by preventing slippage.
source: DNA molecules showing full unwinding did not show any slippage events, suggesting a novel function of DnaG that stimulates unwinding by preventing slippage.
evidence: This is an inference from the observation that slippage is absent with DnaG.

claim: Stalling events were still observed in the presence of DnaG, but were less pronounced.
source: Stalling events were still observed in the presence of DnaG, but were less pronounced (Figure 3—figure supplement 1).
evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 3—figure supplement 1.

claim: Presence of other replication proteins may further assist the helicase unwinding activity.
source: Presence of other replication proteins may further assist the helicase unwinding activity (Stano et al., 2005).
evidence: This is speculation supported by citation.

claim: Slippage was observed using the 40 AT DNA but less frequently than with GC base pairs.
source: Slippage was also observed using the 40 AT DNA but less frequently (Figure 3b).
evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 3b.

claim: T7 gp4, E1 and Rho helicase have higher affinities to ssNA in the nucleotide-bound state.
source: Because T7 gp4, E1 and Rho helicase have higher affinities to ssNA in the nucleotide-bound state (Adelman et al., 2006; Enemark and Joshua-Tor, 2006; Hingorani and Patel, 1993; Thomsen and Berger, 2009) we hypothesized that slippage would occur more frequently at lower ATP concentrations.
evidence: This is supported by citations to previous studies.

claim: At sub-saturating ATP concentrations, a significant increase of slippage events was observed.
source: Indeed, at sub-saturating ATP concentrations we observed a significant increase of slippage events (Figure 3c) and the number of slippage events before complete unwinding increased for decreasing ATP concentrations (Figure 3d).
evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 3c and 3d.

claim: The number of slippage events before complete unwinding increased for decreasing ATP concentrations.
source: Indeed, at sub-saturating ATP concentrations we observed a significant increase of slippage events (Figure 3c) and the number of slippage events before complete unwinding increased for decreasing ATP concentrations (Figure 3d).
evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 3d.

claim: Inclusion of ADP in the reaction did not reduce or increase the slippage events significantly.
source: Inclusion of ADP in the reaction did not reduce or increase the slippage events significantly, indicating that the enzyme binds tightly to the DNA in both ATP and ADP bound states.
evidence: This is supported by experimental observations.

claim: The enzyme binds tightly to the DNA in both ATP and ADP bound states.
source: Inclusion of ADP in the reaction did not reduce or increase the slippage events significantly, indicating that the enzyme binds tightly to the DNA in both ATP and ADP bound states.
evidence: This is an inference from the observation that ADP does not affect slippage.

claim: The presence of DnaG significantly reduced the average number of slippage events per full unwinding (≈2.5 fold) compared to G40P alone at all tested ATP concentrations.
source: However, the presence of DnaG significantly reduced the average number of slippage events per full unwinding (≈2.5 fold) compared to G40P alone at all tested ATP concentrations (Figure 3d, black triangles and Supplementary file 1 - Table S3).
evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 3d and Supplementary file 1 - Table S3.

claim: The average unwinding time of the AT substrate with or without DnaG at saturating ATP conditions did not change.
source: Interestingly, the average unwinding time of the AT substrate with or without DnaG at saturating ATP conditions did not change.
evidence: This is supported by experimental observations.

claim: ATPγS is a slowly hydrolysable analogue of ATP.
source: ATPγS is a slowly hydrolysable analogue of ATP, and both nucleotides have nearly identical dissociation constants for G40P binding as tested using Mant-ADP (see Materials and methods and Figure 3—figure supplement 1).
evidence: This is established knowledge about ATPγS.

claim: ATP and ATPγS have nearly identical dissociation constants for G40P binding.
source: ATPγS is a slowly hydrolysable analogue of ATP, and both nucleotides have nearly identical dissociation constants for G40P binding as tested using Mant-ADP (see Materials and methods and Figure 3—figure supplement 1).
evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 3—figure supplement 1.

claim: The unwinding rate of 40 bp decreased as the ATPγS concentration increased.
source: As expected, the unwinding rate of 40 bp, kunw, decreased as the ATPγS concentration increased (Figure 3—figure supplement 1).
evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 3—figure supplement 1.

claim: Unwinding traces with 2.5% ATPγS showed a pronounced stalling event that was rarely detected without ATPγS.
source: Close examination of the unwinding traces with 2.5% ATPγS showed a pronounced stalling event that was rarely detected without ATPγS (Figure 4a).
evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 4a.

claim: The stall during unwinding with ATPγS was observed at broadly distributed FRET levels, suggesting the stall occurs stochastically, not at a particular location on DNA.
source: The stall during unwinding was observed at broadly distributed FRET levels (Figure 4e), suggesting the stall occurs stochastically, not at a particular location on DNA.
evidence: This is an inference from the broad distribution of FRET levels shown in Figure 4e.

claim: At elevated ATPγS (≥20% ATPγS) no unwinding reaction was observed.
source: At elevated ATPγS (≥20% ATPγS) no unwinding reaction was observed.
evidence: This is supported by experimental observations.

claim: The lifetime of the first stall during unwinding with ATPγS was 0.44 s ± 0.01 s, independent of ATPγS percentage.
source: The lifetime of the first stall during unwinding was 0.44 s ± 0.01 s, independent of ATPγS percentage (Figure 4c), suggesting that the stall occurs when the enzyme is bound by a well-defined number of ATPγS.
evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 4c.

claim: The stall occurs when the enzyme is bound by a well-defined number of ATPγS.
source: The lifetime of the first stall during unwinding was 0.44 s ± 0.01 s, independent of ATPγS percentage (Figure 4c), suggesting that the stall occurs when the enzyme is bound by a well-defined number of ATPγS.
evidence: This is an inference from the independence of stall lifetime on ATPγS concentration.

claim: The stalled fraction increased linearly between 0.125% and 1% ATPγS, indicating that the stall is caused by a single ATPγS.
source: The stalled fraction increased linearly between 0.125% and 1% ATPγS (Figure 4d, Figure 3—figure supplement 1 and Materials and methods), indicating that the stall is caused by a single ATPγS.
evidence: This is an inference from the linear dependence of stalling on ATPγS concentration.

claim: A random ATP hydrolysis mechanism as observed for ClpX can be excluded for G40P.
source: A random ATP hydrolysis mechanism as observed for ClpX, a AAA+ protein unfolding machine (Martin et al., 2005), can thus be excluded for G40P.
evidence: This is an inference from the single ATPγS stalling result, with citation for comparison.

claim: The model of a concerted ATP hydrolysis is very unlikely to apply to G40P.
source: The model of a concerted ATP hydrolysis is very unlikely to apply to G40P considering the following results of our experiments: (i) The unwinding rate kunw versus ATP relation followed the Michaelis-Menten relation with a Hill coefficient close to 1, indicating that per enzymatic cycle only one ATP has to bind the enzyme (see Materials and methods). (ii) Our slippage data indicate that an ATP or ADP free helicase loses grip to the tracking strand and slips backward. A concerted ATP hydrolysis leads to an ATP/ADP free helicase and an elevated probability to slip backwards at every unwound bp, which would be highly inefficient.
evidence: This is an inference from multiple experimental observations including Hill coefficient and slippage data.

claim: The unwinding rate kunw versus ATP relation followed the Michaelis-Menten relation with a Hill coefficient close to 1, indicating that per enzymatic cycle only one ATP has to bind the enzyme.
source: The model of a concerted ATP hydrolysis is very unlikely to apply to G40P considering the following results of our experiments: (i) The unwinding rate kunw versus ATP relation followed the Michaelis-Menten relation with a Hill coefficient close to 1, indicating that per enzymatic cycle only one ATP has to bind the enzyme (see Materials and methods).
evidence: This is an inference from the Hill coefficient analysis of experimental data.

claim: Slippage data indicate that an ATP or ADP free helicase loses grip to the tracking strand and slips backward.
source: Our slippage data indicate that an ATP or ADP free helicase loses grip to the tracking strand and slips backward.
evidence: This is an inference from the slippage observations at low ATP concentrations.

claim: A concerted ATP hydrolysis leads to an ATP/ADP free helicase and an elevated probability to slip backwards at every unwound bp, which would be highly inefficient.
source: A concerted ATP hydrolysis leads to an ATP/ADP free helicase and an elevated probability to slip backwards at every unwound bp, which would be highly inefficient.
evidence: This is an inference based on the mechanism of concerted hydrolysis and observed slippage behavior.

claim: Sequential nucleotide hydrolysis during ssNA translocation by hexameric helicases is well supported by structural analysis.
source: Sequential nucleotide hydrolysis during ssNA translocation by hexameric helicases is also well supported by structural analysis (Enemark and Joshua-Tor, 2006; Thomsen and Berger, 2009) and was also observed in ssDNA translocation by T7gp4 (Crampton et al., 2006; Liao et al., 2005; Pandey and Patel, 2014).
evidence: This is supported by citations to structural and experimental studies.

claim: Sequential nucleotide hydrolysis was observed in ssDNA translocation by T7gp4.
source: Sequential nucleotide hydrolysis during ssNA translocation by hexameric helicases is also well supported by structural analysis (Enemark and Joshua-Tor, 2006; Thomsen and Berger, 2009) and was also observed in ssDNA translocation by T7gp4 (Crampton et al., 2006; Liao et al., 2005; Pandey and Patel, 2014).
evidence: This is supported by citations to experimental studies.

claim: An optical tweezers study on T7gp4 proposed a sequential nucleotide hydrolysis after analyzing the slippage probability at various nucleotide conditions.
source: An optical tweezers study on T7gp4 proposed a sequential nucleotide hydrolysis after analyzing the slippage probability at various nucleotide conditions (Sun et al., 2011).
evidence: This is supported by citation to Sun et al., 2011.

claim: This study shows the first direct evidence for sequential hydrolysis during DNA unwinding.
source: Here we show the first direct evidence for sequential hydrolysis during DNA unwinding.
evidence: This is a claim about the novelty of the current study's findings.

claim: In the ATP and ADP bound state, G40P has a high affinity to the tracking strand.
source: In the ATP and ADP bound state, G40P has a high affinity to the tracking strand.
evidence: This is an inference from the slippage data and nucleotide binding experiments.

claim: After ADP is released from one subunit the affinity of a central DNA-binding loop to the DNA backbone is reduced.
source: After ADP is released from one subunit the affinity of a central DNA-binding loop to the DNA backbone is reduced (Figure 5a) (Enemark and Joshua-Tor, 2006; Thomsen and Berger, 2009).
evidence: This is an inference from structural studies cited and illustrated in Figure 5a.

claim: The DNA-binding loop moves and contacts the backbone phosphate of the next base pair to be unwound when an ATP binds to the subunit.
source: This loop then moves and contacts the backbone phosphate of the next base pair to be unwound when an ATP binds to the subunit.
evidence: This is part of the proposed mechanistic model based on structural and experimental data.

claim: If the next base pair is an AT base pair, it melts rapidly and the relief of the structural distortion within the enzyme catapults the protein forward by one base pair.
source: If the next base pair is an AT base pair, it melts rapidly and the relief of the structural distortion within the enzyme catapults the protein forward by one base pair.
evidence: This is part of the proposed mechanistic model.

claim: In the case of a GC base pair, the melting step may be significantly slower, preventing a second DNA-binding loop from contacting the next base pair to be unwound because of steric constraints within the narrow central channel.
source: However, in the case of a GC base pair, the melting step may be significantly slower, preventing a second DNA-binding loop from contacting the next base pair to be unwound because of steric constraints within the narrow central channel (Figure 5b).
evidence: This is part of the proposed mechanistic model to explain GC-induced stalling.

claim: A structural study of SV40 LTag helicase suggested that unwinding does not occur by strand exclusion and the duplex DNA squeezes through the central pore.
source: A structural study of SV40 LTag helicase suggested that unwinding does not occur by strand exclusion and the duplex DNA squeezes through the central pore (Li et al., 2003).
evidence: This is supported by citation to Li et al., 2003.

claim: If duplex DNA squeezes through the central pore, the helicase may continue to step forward on the tracking strand without having to wait for duplex melting and may lead to unwinding of multiple base pairs in a burst after several nt translocation.
source: In this case, the helicase may continue to step forward on the tracking strand without having to wait for duplex melting and may lead to unwinding of multiple base pairs in a burst after several nt translocation as has been proposed for a non-hexameric helicase (Myong et al., 2007).
evidence: This is speculation about an alternative mechanism, with citation for comparison.

claim: The unwinding initiation rate increased linearly with protein concentration.
source: The unwinding initiation rate, defined as the inverse of average tinit, increased linearly with protein concentration (Figure 1—figure supplement 1d).
evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 1—figure supplement 1d.

claim: The average unwinding time did not show a significant dependence on protein concentration.
source: In contrast, the average tunw did not show a significant dependence on protein concentration (inset Figure 1—figure supplement 1d).
evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 1—figure supplement 1d inset.

claim: The linear relation between the protein concentration and the initiation rate indicates that G40P is loaded as a preassembled hexamer instead of being assembled on the DNA in situ.
source: The linear relation between the protein concentration and the initiation rate indicates that G40P is loaded as a preassembled hexamer instead of being assembled on the DNA in situ.
evidence: This is an inference from the linear concentration dependence.

claim: Blocking the free ssDNA end of the forked DNA with anti-digoxigenin reduced the percentage of single-molecule FRET traces that show unwinding events from 42% to 4.7%.
source: At [ATP]=1 mM and [G40P6]=60 nM, the percentage of single-molecule FRET traces that show unwinding events was reduced from 42% to 4.7% after incubation of the digoxigenin modified DNA construct with [anti-digoxigenin]=0.1 mg/mL followed by washing out of unbound anti-digoxigenin (Figure 1—figure supplement 1e).
evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 1—figure supplement 1e.

claim: The unwinding rate kunw vs. ATP concentration curve could be well-fitted using the Michaelis-Menten equation, yielding an apparent Michaelis-Menten constant Km = 87 ± 9 µM and a maximum unwinding rate kunw = 1.91 ± 0.05 s−1.
source: The unwinding rate kunw, defined as the inverse of average tunw, vs. ATP concentration (red squares Figure 1—figure supplement 1h) curve could be well-fitted using the Michaelis-Menten equation, yielding an apparent Michaelis-Menten constant Km = 87 ± 9 µM and a maximum unwinding rate kunw = 1.91 ± 0.05 s−1.
evidence: This is derived from fitting experimental data shown in Figure 1—figure supplement 1h.

claim: Including ADP in the reaction increased the apparent Km to 191 ± 14 µM and 272 ± 36 µM at 0.5 mM and 1 mM ADP, respectively.
source: Including ADP in the reaction increased the apparent Km to 191 ± 14 µM and 272 ± 36 µM at 0.5 mM and 1 mM ADP, respectively (Figure 1—figure supplement 1g and h) with little change in the maximum unwinding rate kunw([ADP]=0.5 mM)=2.01 ± 0.04 s−1 and kunw([ADP]=1 mM)=1.91 ± 0.07 s−1.
evidence: This is derived from fitting experimental data with ADP present.

claim: A fit to the Hill-equation to the ATP titration results in a Hill coefficient n = 1.2 ± 0.2.
source: A fit to the more general Hill-equation to the ATP titration results in a Hill coefficient n = 1.2 ± 0.2 (dashed line in Figure 1—figure supplement 1h).
evidence: This is derived from fitting experimental data shown in Figure 1—figure supplement 1h.

claim: A Hill coefficient of 1 implies that either each identical subunit can bind ATP and hydrolyze completely independent of each other or that for every step one or more subunits can bind ATP successively and in coordination but not cooperatively.
source: A Hill coefficient of 1 implies that either each identical subunit can bind ATP and hydrolyze completely independent of each other (no binding cooperativity between the subunits) or that for every step one or more subunits can bind ATP successively and in coordination but not cooperatively (Schnitzer and Block, 1997).
evidence: This is an interpretation of the Hill coefficient with citation for support.

claim: A Hill coefficient of 1 does not imply that only one ATP is bound per enzymatic cycle, but that binding of one ATP neither facilitates nor hinders binding of more ATP.
source: It is important to note that a Hill coefficient of 1 does not imply that only one ATP is bound per enzymatic cycle, but that binding of one ATP neither facilitates nor hinders binding of more ATP (Moffitt et al., 2009).
evidence: This is an interpretation of the Hill coefficient with citation for support.

claim: G40P showed without ssDNA a significant ATPase activity that could be increased after addition of ssDNA.
source: We observed without any ssDNA present in solution a significant ATPase activity. Addition of ssDNA to the solution increased the ATPase activity of G40P by a factor of two.
evidence: This is supported by experimental data from the ATPase assay.

claim: The ATPase activity of G40P without ssDNA was successfully suppressed by exchanging MgCl2 to MnCl2.
source: The ATPase activity of G40P without ssDNA was successfully suppressed by exchanging MgCl2 to MnCl2.
evidence: This is supported by experimental data from the ATPase assay.

claim: ATP and ATPγS showed similar affinity for G40P (ATPγS KD = 1.4 ± 0.9 µM, ATP KD = 3.5 ± 0.8 µM).
source: Both ligands showed similar affinity (ATPγS KD = 1.4 ± 0.9 µM, ATP KD = 3.5 ± 0.8 µM).
evidence: This is derived from competitive titration experiments with mant-ADP.
